newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone forces secure key spots in city centre.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone forces secure key spots in city centre.

text.p: Sierra Leone rebels allied to coup leaders massed around a Freetown hotel guarded by Nigerian troops on Monday after Nigeria launched a strike against the coup.

Hotel guests and Nigerian soldiers said the Nigerians were hopelessly outnumbered and the beachside hotel near the Sierra Leone military headquarters was about to be overrun. "It's a fight for survival," said one Nigerian officer.
In the city centre, Revolutionary United Front rebels and Sierra Leone soldiers secured strategic positions in anticipation of an attack, though Nigerian troops were nowhere to be seen.
Several thousand people protested against the Nigerians, saying they did not support the May 25 military coup, but they opposed any foreign intervention.

Nigerian ships in the bay west of Freetown began a bombardment at daybreak after talks between Nigerian and British diplomats and the coup leaders at the seafront military headquarters collapsed on Sunday night.
The bombardment was still going on some five hours later, and small arms fire could be heard outside the hotel and from the area around the military headquarters.

The Mammy Yoko Hotel holds about 1,000 West African foreigners who took refuge there after the coup and a few foreign journalists. Hundreds of foreigners fleeing looting and violence have been evacuated from the heliport in its grounds in the past few days.
Civilians took refuge in the hotel basement. The building's first and second floor windows were shattered by incoming fire and four Nigerian soldiers were lightly wounded.
The Nigerians said they took over the international airport at Lungi, north of the capital, which had been under uneasy joint control since the coup.
"We took it this morning. There was a firefight with the Sierra Leonean forces there but it didn't last long at all," a Nigerian commander told Reuters.
He said Lungi airport would be used to bring in reinforcements for the intervention to restore Sierra Leone's elected government.
The booming of naval guns shook the capital at 6 a.m. (0600 GMT) as Nigerian vessels opened fire.

A Reuters reporter saw the bodies of a couple and their grandson in the Aberdeen district who neighbours said had been killed when a mortar shell from the Nigerian ships hit their house. There was no other sign of shells hitting targets.

Nigeria, Ghana and Guinea sent troops to Sierra Leone after the coup, ready for a strike if talks with Major Johnny Paul Koromah and his Armed Forces Revolutionary Council failed. They are thought to have about 3,000 men in Freetown.
Journalists in the hotel saw a jet of the Guinean air force bombing RUF positions.

A Nigerian diplomat said Monday's attack followed a breakdown of last-minute negotiations that went on late into Sunday night. "Each time we reached an agreement, the chairman was nowhere to be found to sign it," he said.

In Harare on Monday to attend a summit of his Organisation of African Unity, Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim said: "In the interest of Sierra Leone and Africa as a whole, everything must be done to restore constitutional legality in that country."
On Sunday, Koromah announced his 20-member council, with rebel leader Foday Sankoh as vice chairman and including three more members of Sankoh's RUF.
A senior diplomat said Sankoh's rebels, who have been fighting a bush war since 1991 and have allied with the coup makers, opposed a settlement and had not been in the talks.
Sankoh is in detention at a hotel in the Nigerian capital. His telephone was cut off after he called on his rebels to fight alongside the army.
